title: Unit 6: Gene Expression and Regulation

topics.name: DNA and RNA structure and DNA replication
Regulation of gene expression and cell specialization

guide.title: Gene expression and regulation: review guide
guide.intro: DNA stores the instructions for making proteins. This unit follows DNA replication, transcription, and translation, explains how cells control which genes are expressed, and covers mutations and the biotechnology used to study and change DNA.

sections.title: DNA and RNA structure and DNA replication
body: DNA is a double helix of antiparallel strands with A–T and G–C base pairs, so A = T and G = C in amounts. Prokaryotes usually have a circular chromosome and may carry plasmids (small, extra circular DNA molecules); eukaryotes have linear chromosomes.

Replication is semiconservative: each new double helix has one old strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds the DNA, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end of a growing strand, the leading strand is made continuously, and the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments that ligase joins together.
points: If a DNA sample is 30% A, it is also 30% T, leaving 20% G and 20% C.
Primers (RNA) give DNA polymerase a starting point.

sections.title: Transcription, RNA processing, and translation
body: Transcription: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′ → 5′ and builds mRNA 5′ → 3′, pairing U with A. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is processed: introns are removed (splicing), a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail are added. Alternative splicing lets one gene code for several proteins.

Translation: at a ribosome, each mRNA codon (three bases) pairs with a tRNA anticodon, and the tRNA brings the matching amino acid. The ribosome joins the amino acids with peptide bonds, from the start codon AUG until a stop codon.
points: The genetic code is redundant: several codons can code for the same amino acid.
Prokaryotes can transcribe and translate at the same time.
mRNA is complementary to the template strand.

sections.title: Regulation of gene expression and cell specialization
body: In bacteria, operons group genes under one promoter. The lac operon is inducible: lactose inactivates the repressor, so the genes are transcribed. The trp operon is repressible: tryptophan activates the repressor, which shuts off transcription when tryptophan is plentiful.

In eukaryotes, transcription factors binding to promoters and enhancers, DNA methylation (usually silencing), and histone acetylation (usually activating) control which genes are expressed. Every cell in an organism has the same genes; cells specialize by expressing different subsets of them.
points: Regulation saves energy by making proteins only when they are needed.
Small RNAs can block translation of specific mRNAs.
Differences in transcription factors explain why liver and skin cells make different proteins.

sections.title: Mutations and biotechnology
body: Mutations change the DNA sequence. A substitution can be silent (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid), or nonsense (a stop codon). An insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three shifts the reading frame and changes every codon after it. Mutations provide the variation that natural selection acts on.

Biotechnology: PCR copies DNA (doubling it each cycle); gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size, with smaller fragments moving farther; transformation inserts plasmids into bacteria, often with an antibiotic-resistance gene so transformed cells can be selected; DNA sequencing reads the order of bases.
points: Frameshifts are usually more harmful than single substitutions.
After n PCR cycles, one molecule becomes 2ⁿ copies.
DNA is negatively charged, so it moves toward the positive electrode.

example.prompt: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGA-5′. Write the mRNA and the first codon's amino acid.
example.solution: Pair each base (T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C): the mRNA is 5′-AUGCCU-3′. The first codon, AUG, is the start codon and codes for methionine.

misconceptions: They have the same genes but express different ones.
Many are silent or neutral, and some are beneficial.
“DNA polymerase can add nucleotides to either end.”
It adds only to the 3′ end.
“In gel electrophoresis, larger fragments move farther.”
Smaller fragments move farther through the gel.

questions.prompt: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percent is guanine?
questions.explanation: A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60% and G + C = 40%, split equally: G = 20%.
choiceExplanations: 30% is the amount of thymine, which pairs with adenine.
40% is G + C together.
70% is everything except adenine.

questions.prompt: DNA replication is semiconservative. What does that mean?
choices: One new double helix is entirely original and the other entirely new
Both strands of each new double helix are new
Each new double helix has one original strand and one new strand
Only half of the DNA is copied
questions.explanation: Each original strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.
choiceExplanations: That would be conservative replication, which experiments ruled out.
Each new molecule keeps one old strand.
The whole genome is copied.

questions.prompt: Why is the lagging strand made in short Okazaki fragments?
choices: Ligase cuts the strand into pieces
Helicase unwinds that strand more slowly
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end, so on that strand it must work away from the replication fork
The lagging strand has no template
questions.explanation: The strands are antiparallel. On one strand, 5′ → 3′ synthesis runs away from the fork, so it is made in pieces as the fork opens.
choiceExplanations: Ligase joins fragments; it doesn't cut them.
Helicase unwinds both strands at once.
Both strands serve as templates.

questions.prompt: What would build up in a cell that has no working DNA ligase?
choices: Unwound but uncopied DNA
Extra RNA primers on the leading strand only
Double-stranded RNA
Unjoined Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand
questions.explanation: Ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments. Without it, the lagging strand stays in pieces.
choiceExplanations: Helicase and polymerase still work, so the DNA is copied.
Primers are removed and replaced by other enzymes; the leading strand needs few joins.
Ligase isn't involved in making RNA.

questions.prompt: Many bacteria carry plasmids. What are plasmids?
choices: Small circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome
Linear chromosomes in a nucleus
Ribosomes found in bacteria
Proteins that copy DNA
questions.explanation: Plasmids are extra circular DNA molecules that often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.
choiceExplanations: Bacteria have no nucleus, and plasmids are circular.
Ribosomes are made of RNA and protein.
DNA polymerase copies DNA.

questions.prompt: In a eukaryotic cell, where does transcription take place and what does it make?
choices: At the ribosome; it makes DNA
In the cytoplasm; it makes protein from mRNA
In the mitochondria; it makes ATP
In the nucleus; it makes RNA from a DNA template
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase transcribes genes into RNA inside the nucleus.
choiceExplanations: Ribosomes make protein, not DNA.
That describes translation.
Mitochondria make ATP by respiration.

questions.prompt: The DNA template strand 3′-TAC-5′ is transcribed. What is the mRNA codon?
questions.explanation: Pair T→A, A→U, C→G; the mRNA runs antiparallel to the template, so it reads 5′-AUG-3′.
choiceExplanations: The mRNA's 5′ end pairs with the template's 3′ end.
UAC copies the template's letters instead of pairing them.
RNA uses uracil, not thymine.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Which change happens to eukaryotic pre-mRNA before it leaves the nucleus?
choices: Introns are removed, and a 5′ cap and poly-A tail are added
Amino acids are attached to it
Exons are removed
Thymine replaces uracil
questions.explanation: RNA processing splices out introns and adds the cap and tail, which protect the mRNA and help ribosomes bind.
choiceExplanations: Amino acids are attached to tRNA, not mRNA.
Exons are the parts that are kept.
RNA contains uracil, and processing doesn't swap bases.

questions.prompt: During translation, what pairs with each mRNA codon?
choices: An amino acid directly
A DNA nucleotide
The anticodon of a tRNA carrying an amino acid
A ribosomal protein
questions.explanation: tRNA anticodons base-pair with codons, bringing the matching amino acid into place.
choiceExplanations: Amino acids don't pair with codons; tRNAs carry them.
DNA isn't involved in translation.
Ribosomal proteins help, but codons pair with tRNA.

questions.prompt: Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes but make far more different proteins. Which process best explains this?
choices: Crossing over during mitosis
Alternative splicing, which joins different combinations of exons from the same gene
DNA replication
Each gene being translated into exactly one protein
questions.explanation: Different splicing patterns produce several mRNAs, and so several proteins, from one gene.
choiceExplanations: Crossing over occurs in meiosis and doesn't create new proteins from one gene.
Replication copies DNA; it doesn't make proteins.
That would give only as many proteins as genes.

questions.prompt: A person's liver cells and skin cells contain:
choices: The same genes, all expressed equally
Completely different genes
No genes once they specialize
The same genes, but they express different subsets of them
questions.explanation: Body cells have the same DNA; regulation of gene expression makes them different.
choiceExplanations: Different cells express different genes.
Body cells share the same genome.
Specialized cells keep their DNA.

questions.prompt: In E. coli, what happens to the lac operon when lactose is present?
choices: Lactose inactivates the repressor, so the genes for digesting lactose are transcribed
Lactose is used as the RNA polymerase
Lactose activates the repressor and blocks transcription
The genes are deleted
questions.explanation: The lac operon is inducible: lactose (as allolactose) binds the repressor and releases it from the operator.
choiceExplanations: Lactose is a sugar, not an enzyme.
That describes a repressible operon such as trp.
Regulation changes expression, not the DNA.

questions.prompt: How do DNA methylation and histone acetylation usually affect gene expression?
choices: Methylation activates genes; acetylation silences them
Methylation tends to silence genes; acetylation tends to activate them
Both change the DNA sequence
Both always activate genes
questions.explanation: Methylated DNA is packed tightly and less accessible; acetylated histones loosen chromatin so transcription can happen.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the usual effects.
These are epigenetic changes; the base sequence stays the same.
They usually have opposite effects.

questions.prompt: The trp operon makes the enzymes that synthesize tryptophan. What happens when tryptophan is abundant in the cell?
choices: Tryptophan inactivates the repressor, so transcription increases
Tryptophan binds and activates the repressor, which blocks transcription of the operon
Tryptophan breaks down the RNA polymerase
The operon is transcribed faster to use up tryptophan
questions.explanation: The trp operon is repressible: its end product turns it off, so the cell stops making enzymes it doesn't need.
choiceExplanations: That describes the inducible lac operon.
Tryptophan acts through the repressor, not by destroying enzymes.
Making more enzymes would waste energy when tryptophan is plentiful.

questions.prompt: A substitution changes a codon, but the protein's amino acid sequence stays the same. What kind of mutation is this?
choices: A nonsense mutation
A frameshift mutation
A missense mutation
A silent mutation
questions.explanation: The genetic code is redundant, so the new codon can code for the same amino acid.
choiceExplanations: A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon.
A frameshift is caused by an insertion or deletion.
A missense mutation changes the amino acid.

questions.prompt: Why is inserting one extra base near the start of a gene usually more harmful than substituting one base?
choices: It shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
It changes only one amino acid
It always creates a start codon
Extra bases are removed during splicing
questions.explanation: Codons are read in groups of three, so a one-base insertion changes how all later bases are grouped.
choiceExplanations: That describes a substitution.
An insertion doesn't necessarily create a start codon.
Splicing removes introns, not mutations.

questions.prompt: In gel electrophoresis, how are DNA fragments separated?
choices: By size: smaller fragments move farther toward the positive electrode
By base sequence alone
By charge: positive fragments move farther
By size: larger fragments move farther
questions.explanation: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive end; shorter fragments slip through the gel faster.
choiceExplanations: Fragments of the same length move together whatever their sequence.
All DNA fragments are negatively charged.
Larger fragments are slowed more by the gel.

questions.prompt: Bacteria are mixed with a plasmid carrying a gene for ampicillin resistance, and only a few take it up. How can you identify the transformed bacteria?
choices: Grow them without ampicillin and keep the largest colonies
Grow them on plates containing ampicillin; only bacteria with the plasmid survive
Count which bacteria divide fastest
Run them on a gel to see which are heavier
questions.explanation: The resistance gene acts as a selectable marker: ampicillin kills bacteria without the plasmid.
choiceExplanations: Without the antibiotic, all bacteria grow, so it doesn't select.
Growth rate doesn't show which cells took up the plasmid.
Gels separate DNA fragments, not living bacteria.
